body.text: As James Curran’s excellent new book, Grand Ambition, makes clear, Paul Keating was from the outset focused on the “big picture” and saw APEC primarily as a vehicle for managing regional tensions. While this goal seems closer to realisation, it is not clear whether Australia will get any credit for this, or benefit from the possible outcome of the talks either.

The prospect of the “great powers” getting together to make deals over the heads of the region’s lesser lights is not how things were supposed to develop. Neither Keating nor APEC can be blamed for this, though. Rather, it reflects the inability of multilateral organisations like APEC and the United Nations to become more inclusive forums in which a range of hitherto overlooked or ignored voices can be heard.

So-called “realists” will no doubt argue that it was ever thus, and that power is the only currency that matters in determining international political, economic and especially strategic outcomes. Perhaps so, but the world currently faces unprecedented threats, like rapidly accelerating environmental breakdown, that can only be addressed by widespread cooperation and collective action. APEC’s primary goal of encouraging greater, less regulated economic integration and development seems anachronistic in this context.

One area of potential hope, however, in which APEC’s mainly middle power membership might encourage useful cooperation and action, is in responding to the equally urgent challenge posed by artificial intelligence. Not only is it entirely possible that the AI bubble may pop and plunge the region into yet another economic crisis, AI also poses a direct threat to the lives and livelihoods of people across the Asia-Pacific.

AI featured in the Gyeongju Declaration of APEC’s 2025 summit in South Korea. As is the way with APEC, there is a continuing focus on the possible economic benefits of AI, but there is also a recognition that it is going to have significant and differing impacts on the Asia-Pacific labour force and demand for energy. And yet, APEC has neither the mandate nor the capacity to deal with the sometimes perverse effects of unconstrained economic or technological development.
